newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Iraq oil could move by mid-December - Hiti.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil could move by mid-December - Hiti.

text.p: Head of the Iraqi OPEC delegation Osama al-Hiti said that renewed Iraqi oil exports could move by mid-December.
"Mid December is very realistic if they move fast," he told a news briefing after Thursday's OPEC meeting.

He said that state oil company SOMO had already sent out invitations to oil companies to come to Baghdad for negotiations on oil contract terms. Hiti said he expected to start meeting oil executives in about a week or two. These included "most of the companies we used to do business with."
After terms were agreed with companies, oil experts can begin as soon as the U.N. Secretary-General reports to the Security Council and oil monitors are in place in Iraq.
Hiti said there were no technical obstacles in the way and that the metering station at Mina al Bakr port had been upgraded to meet a request by U.N. inspectors.
Hiti said that Iraq would stick with the terms of the U.N. deal, which allows exports of up to $2 billion for six months, but would then seek an increase in this amount.

"We have every intention of carrying on with the U.N. for six months. But then definitely we would be asking for a higher amount. Six dollars per capita, per month is not enough, even for the basic medicines that are needed," he said.

He also reiterated Iraq's long-standing committment to its pre-Gulf War OPEC quota of 3.14 million barrels per day and said Iraq ultimately would seek parity with Iran, but he said this would be subject to future negotiations within OPEC.

"Due to the situation we have faced in the last six years there is complete understanding among ministers that we have to sit and discuss how we will increase our output. But we don't want to upset the market," he said.
Hiti said that the OPEC meeting that ended today decided that a six month output rollover was the best course of action in the current situation.

"All the delegates...were at ease, hoping that we would come on the market as soon as possible," he said. "There was a feeling that we have been waiting for Iraq for so long to come onto the market and it would relieve some of the uncertainty."
However the ministers did not consider a one year rollover because "we wanted to wait and see after April when demand goes down and prices are likely to follow," he said.
